introduction-runtime-kernel-tuning.core: The kernel exposes hundreds of tunables through /proc/sys (sysctl): network buffers and backlogs, VM behaviour (swappiness, dirty ratios, overcommit), filesystem limits (file-max, inotify), and kernel behaviour (pid_max, panic settings). Changing them takes effect immediately without reboot, and persisting them in /etc/sysctl.d makes them survive restarts. Tune from measured bottlenecks, one change at a time, and document why.

first_principles.problem: A team copies a 'Linux performance tuning' blog's 50 sysctls into production and introduces instability.

analogy.title: Adjusting a mixing desk during a concert
analogy.story: Small, deliberate tweaks while listening, not pushing every fader to max.
analogy.breaks: Sound engineers hear instantly; some tunable effects only show under load.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Change applied and persistent, with rationale.

code.text:
sysctl net.core.somaxconn
sysctl -w net.core.somaxconn=4096
cat > /etc/sysctl.d/90-web.conf <<'EOF'
# bursty accept queue for nginx (INC-1832)
net.core.somaxconn = 4096
EOF
sysctl --system

check.q: Where should persistent sysctl settings be stored on modern distros?
check.a: In drop-in files under /etc/sysctl.d/, applied with sysctl --system at boot.

cpu-bound-vs-io-bound.core: CPU-bound work is limited by computation: high user or system CPU and the run queue full; speed it up with more or faster cores, better algorithms, or parallelism. I/O-bound work is limited by waiting for disk or network: low CPU, high iowait or blocked tasks, latency in storage or remote calls; speed it up with faster I/O, caching, concurrency and async I/O. Misdiagnosing the type leads to useless fixes, such as adding CPUs to a disk-bound job.

first_principles.problem: A team doubles the CPU count of a slow ETL job, and it runs at the same speed.
truths: CPU and I/O waits look different.

analogy.title: A kitchen slowed by cooks vs by deliveries
analogy.story: If chefs are overwhelmed, hire chefs; if they're waiting for ingredients, fix deliveries.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens are visible; bottlenecks need metrics.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Disk is the bottleneck; add caching instead of CPUs.

code.text:
vmstat 1 5
#  r  b   us sy id wa
#  1 12    8  4 40 48   ← blocked tasks + iowait → I/O-bound
pidstat -d 1 3 | sort -k6 -n | tail -3    # top disk readers/writers
cat /proc/pressure/io

check.q: What vmstat signs indicate an I/O-bound workload?
check.a: High wa (iowait) and many processes in the b (blocked) column while CPU user time is low.

load-average-the-most-misinterpreted-met.core: Load average is the number of tasks running, runnable or in uninterruptible I/O sleep, averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. It's meaningful only relative to CPU count and alongside CPU and I/O metrics. Load 4 on 64 cores is idle; load 4 on 2 cores is overloaded. Rising D-state tasks from NFS hangs inflate load without CPU use. Trends (1 vs 15 minutes) show whether a problem is growing or easing.

first_principles.problem: An alert 'load > 10' fires constantly on 96-core servers and is ignored.

analogy.title: People in a bank compared to tellers
analogy.story: Ten people is a crowd with two tellers but nothing with fifty.
analogy.breaks: Banks show queues; load averages smooth over minutes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One threshold works across server sizes.

code.text:
read l1 l5 l15 _ < /proc/loadavg; n=$(nproc)
awk -v l=$l1 -v n=$n 'BEGIN { printf "normalised load: %.2f\n", l/n }'
# PromQL: node_load5 / count without(cpu, mode) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"})

check.q: Is a load average of 8 high?
check.a: It depends on CPU count and context: high for a 2-core machine, low for a 64-core one, and it may reflect I/O waits rather than CPU.

essential-tunables-vm-swappiness.core: Key VM tunables: vm.swappiness biases reclaim between anonymous memory and file cache (lower keeps app memory resident; 10 is common for databases). vm.dirty_ratio and dirty_background_ratio (or the _bytes variants) control how much dirty page cache accumulates before background and then blocking writeback; large values on big-RAM hosts cause huge write stalls. vm.min_free_kbytes reserves memory for atomic allocations, and vm.overcommit_memory sets allocation strictness.

first_principles.problem: A 512 GB server stalls for seconds when 100 GB of dirty pages hit dirty_ratio at 20%.
truths: Percent-based limits scale badly with RAM.

analogy.title: Letting dishes pile up before washing
analogy.story: With a huge kitchen, waiting until 20% of the counter is covered means a massive washing session that stops all cooking.
analogy.breaks: Dishes don't get lost; dirty pages are lost on power failure until written.

example.title: Large-RAM writeback

code.text:
# /etc/sysctl.d/90-vm.conf
vm.swappiness = 10
vm.dirty_background_bytes = 268435456   # 256 MB: start background writeback early
vm.dirty_bytes = 1073741824             # 1 GB: cap before writers block
vm.min_free_kbytes = 1048576

example.outcome: VM tuned to hardware and workload.

check.q: Why use dirty_bytes instead of dirty_ratio on very large-memory servers?
check.a: Percentage thresholds allow enormous amounts of dirty data on big RAM, causing long writeback stalls; byte limits keep flushing bounded.

essential-tunables-network-buffers.core: Network tunables size queues and buffers. net.core.somaxconn and tcp_max_syn_backlog set accept and SYN backlogs; netdev_max_backlog and netdev_budget control the per-CPU receive backlog and softirq budget; rmem_max, wmem_max, tcp_rmem and tcp_wmem set socket buffers for high-BDP paths; ip_local_port_range sets ephemeral ports for many outbound connections; tcp_tw_reuse handles TIME_WAIT reuse for clients; and nf_conntrack_max sizes the connection-tracking table.

first_principles.problem: A busy API gateway drops new connections at peak and exhausts ephemeral ports to backends.

analogy.title: Widening a stadium's entrance queues and parking
analogy.story: More queue space at gates, more parking spaces for departures, and bigger buses for long trips.
analogy.breaks: Stadiums show crowds; drops show only in counters.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No accept drops or port exhaustion at peak.

code.text:
# /etc/sysctl.d/90-gateway.conf
net.core.somaxconn = 8192
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 16384
net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 16384
net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10240 65535
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 1048576

check.q: What happens when a client host exhausts ephemeral ports to one backend?
check.a: New outbound connections to that destination fail (EADDRNOTAVAIL) until ports in TIME_WAIT free up.

the-magic-sysrq-key.core: Magic SysRq lets you send emergency commands directly to the kernel even when userspace is hung, via keyboard (Alt+SysRq+key), serial break, or echo key > /proc/sysrq-trigger. Useful keys: s (sync), u (remount read-only), b (immediate reboot), f (invoke the OOM killer), t (dump task states), w (dump blocked tasks), m (memory info) and c (crash for kdump). The safe reboot sequence is REISUB. Restrict it with kernel.sysrq.

first_principles.problem: A server is unresponsive over SSH but the console works, and the team needs a safe reboot without corrupting disks.
truths: Kernel can act when userspace can't.
derivation: Safe reboot: **R E I S U B**.

analogy.title: An emergency override panel
analogy.story: When normal controls freeze, a sealed panel lets technicians stop the machine safely or record its state.
analogy.breaks: Override panels need physical access; SysRq can also be triggered over /proc.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Diagnostics captured; filesystems synced before reboot.

code.text:
sysctl kernel.sysrq           # e.g. 176 or 1
echo w > /proc/sysrq-trigger  # dump blocked (D) tasks to dmesg
echo m > /proc/sysrq-trigger  # memory info
# last resort safe reboot
for k in s u b; do echo $k > /proc/sysrq-trigger; sleep 2; done

check.q: What does the REISUB sequence do?
check.a: Raw keyboard, tErminate, kIll, Sync, Unmount (remount ro), reBoot, a safe emergency reboot.
